knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(x)\,i+(x + y)\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=5 \cos{\left(t \right)}\,i+8 \sin{\left(t \right)}\,j$ for $t\in[0,2\pi)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the outward flux is

$$\oint_C F\cdot n\,\mathrm ds=\oint_C P\,\mathrm dy-Q\,\mathrm dx,$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$.

Along the curve $C$, we have $x=5 \cos{\left(t \right)}$, $y=8 \sin{\left(t \right)}$.

Therefore, $P=5 \cos{\left(t \right)}$ and $Q=8 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 5 \cos{\left(t \right)}$.

Computing the derivatives gives $x\prime(t)=- 5 \sin{\left(t \right)}$ and $y\prime(t)=8 \cos{\left(t \right)}$.

Finally, evaluate the integral:

$$\begin{aligned}\oint_C F\cdot n\,\mathrm ds&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y\prime-Q x\prime)\,\mathrm dt\\&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left[(5 \cos{\left(t \right)})(8 \cos{\left(t \right)})-(8 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 5 \cos{\left(t \right)})(- 5 \sin{\left(t \right)})\right]\,\mathrm dt\\&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(40 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 25 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)} + 40 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)\,\mathrm dt.\end{aligned}$$

The integrand is $40+25\sin t\cos t$. Use $u=\sin t$, $\mathrm du=\cos t\,\mathrm dt$ in the second term: $$[40t]_0^{2\pi}+25\int_0^0u\,\mathrm du=80 \pi.$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(4 x)\,i+(4 y)\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\,i+8 \sin{\left(t \right)}\,j$ for $t\in[0,2\pi)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the outward flux is

$$\oint_C F\cdot n\,\mathrm ds=\oint_C P\,\mathrm dy-Q\,\mathrm dx,$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$.

Along the curve $C$, we have $x=2 \cos{\left(t \right)}$, $y=8 \sin{\left(t \right)}$.

Therefore, $P=8 \cos{\left(t \right)}$ and $Q=32 \sin{\left(t \right)}$.

Computing the derivatives gives $x\prime(t)=- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}$ and $y\prime(t)=8 \cos{\left(t \right)}$.

Finally, evaluate the integral:

$$\begin{aligned}\oint_C F\cdot n\,\mathrm ds&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y\prime-Q x\prime)\,\mathrm dt\\&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left[(8 \cos{\left(t \right)})(8 \cos{\left(t \right)})-(32 \sin{\left(t \right)})(- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)})\right]\,\mathrm dt\\&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(64 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 64 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)\,\mathrm dt.\end{aligned}$$

Using $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$, the integrand is $64$. Thus the flux is $[64t]_0^{2\pi}=128 \pi$.

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(x y)\,i+(x^{2})\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=10 \cos{\left(t \right)}\,i+10 \sin{\left(t \right)}\,j$ for $t\in[0,2\pi)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the outward flux is

$$\oint_C F\cdot n\,\mathrm ds=\oint_C P\,\mathrm dy-Q\,\mathrm dx,$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$.

Along the curve $C$, we have $x=10 \cos{\left(t \right)}$, $y=10 \sin{\left(t \right)}$.

Therefore, $P=100 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}$ and $Q=100 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}$.

Computing the derivatives gives $x\prime(t)=- 10 \sin{\left(t \right)}$ and $y\prime(t)=10 \cos{\left(t \right)}$.

Finally, evaluate the integral:

$$\begin{aligned}\oint_C F\cdot n\,\mathrm ds&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y\prime-Q x\prime)\,\mathrm dt\\&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left[(100 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)})(10 \cos{\left(t \right)})-(100 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)})(- 10 \sin{\left(t \right)})\right]\,\mathrm dt\\&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(2000 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}\right)\,\mathrm dt.\end{aligned}$$

Use $u=\cos t$, $\mathrm du=-\sin t\,\mathrm dt$: $$-2000\int_1^1u^2\,\mathrm du=0.$$
